raw_response:
I would evaluate **fail2zig first**, with **fail2ban-rs** as the next documented option. Both describe a single added application executable without a Python runtime, and both document blocking repeated SSH password failures. The important distinction is which host tools and Linux setup the chosen configuration requires. These recommendations come from public documentation, not an installation or attack test.

I am interpreting “single binary” as one added blocker executable. Existing SSH, the Linux kernel and ordinary host utilities remain part of the server. If the intent is also to avoid invoking log-reader or firewall helper commands, fail2zig's file-input/native-nftables path is the strongest documented match among the inspected options.

### 1. fail2zig — first option to evaluate

The project combines daemon and administration functions in one executable and explicitly states that Python is unnecessary. It documents SSH password-failure detection and a native nftables backend. For this request, the proposed setup is an SSH-only rule reading the authentication log file and using native nftables. [Project documentation](https://fail2zig.com/)

Check the target platform before deployment: the v0.4.8 installation document identifies Debian 13 x86_64 as its selected live qualification target, while other builds have narrower verification. Journal input calls journalctl, and the iptables/ipset options need their corresponding host tools. The main site and versioned installation text disagree about the oldest supported release; this recommendation is specifically for v0.4.8, not an older-version migration. [Installation scope](https://github.com/ul0gic/fail2zig/blob/v0.4.8/docs/operations/installation.md)

**Judgment: DIRECT_DOCUMENTED for that stated configuration.** It covers the requested replacement scope. Actual host compatibility still needs checking.

### 2. fail2ban-rs — a straightforward option for systemd hosts

Its README documents one static application executable without Python, requires Linux and systemd, and supplies an SSH jail with a retry window and temporary firewall ban. It still invokes the selected host firewall tools. Keep the deployment limited to the SSH jail; optional webhook dependencies are unnecessary for this request. [Official README](https://github.com/aejimmi/fail2ban-rs)

**Judgment: DIRECT_DOCUMENTED within the stated Linux/systemd configuration.** Confirm the host's log format and firewall backend rather than copying the example unchanged. A single application executable is not a claim that the entire server has no other executables.

### 3. reaction — plausible, but packaging needs confirmation

The official tutorial specifically demonstrates watching Linux SSH logs, recognizing unsuccessful password authentication and applying firewall bans. That is the correct operating relationship for the requested task. [SSH tutorial](https://reaction.ppom.me/get-started/tutorial-en/)

The current project describes a Rust daemon, but that alone does not prove its entire runtime dependency set or the number of application executables in a release. The release page was not readable in this run. [Project](https://reaction.ppom.me/) · [Release listing](https://framagit.org/ppom/reaction/-/releases)

**Judgment: INSUFFICIENT, retained for follow-up rather than rejected.** The next decisive check is a release manifest showing one added executable and no required Python. If confirmed, the documented SSH setup becomes a direct fit; if either requirement is violated, that setup should be excluded.

### 4. Existing OpenSSH penalties — check before adding another daemon

OpenSSH 9.8 introduced PerSourcePenalties, which accumulates penalties for repeated unsuccessful authentication and temporarily refuses connections from the source. The release also documents exempt address ranges and cautions about shared addresses. This is a configuration route within an existing supporting SSH server, not a separate single-binary blocker product; the same release explicitly split the server into multiple executables. [OpenSSH 9.8 release](https://www.openssh.org/txt/release-9.8)

**Judgment: INSUFFICIENT until the installed SSH implementation/version is known.** If the relevant options exist and their behavior matches the desired banning policy, this may avoid installing another blocker. If they do not exist, it is not an available replacement on the current host. Keep password authentication available and check emergency access when evaluating any source-based ban policy.

### Why SSHGuard is excluded from this particular shortlist

SSHGuard fits the SSH log-blocking purpose, but its own architecture describes separate log-reader, parser, blocker and firewall-backend programs. That conflicts with the single added application binary requirement. Extra service coverage is not the reason for exclusion. [Official architecture](https://sshguard.net/docs/contributing.html)

### Evidence and date limits

The question is dated August 28, 2026; the searches were performed November 21, 2026. The current fail2zig, fail2ban-rs and reaction pages did not establish their exact feature state on the question date. A search snippet dates fail2ban-rs 1.5.4 to October 5, 2026, so that release metadata is later evidence; an attempted older-version page was inaccessible. OpenSSH 9.8's release is explicitly dated July 1, 2024. I would not describe current live documentation as a verified historical recommendation.

Before replacing the running service, verify that the chosen configuration recognizes the actual SSH failure messages, creates and expires the intended ban, and preserves a usable emergency-management path. Those checks remain to be performed on the servers.
